_Logical Positivism_ is a great book. It combines careful attention to archival records, quantitative data, and social context, to tell an incredibly rich story about the rise, and I guess fall, of logical positivism in America. I'm going to recommend it to all my students as crucial background for how philosophy in America got to where it is, and a correction to several popular narratives.

On the data side, this is one of the best examples you'll see of data use that highlights simple understandable statistics, the main one in the book is simply how often philosophers are mentioned, with awareness of the limits of these statistics. I'll just mention one aspect of this that stuck out. The book often presents tables of outliers, e.g., philosophers who are mentioned most often or (relative to expectation) least often in a particular corpus. Whenever I build tables like that, they are mostly records of where the data needs cleaning. These tables look simple, but the work that goes into making the outliers look meaningful is so demanding, and the results here are fascinating.

The book mentions the social impact of positivism, this is a big focus of chapter 11, and there's a question here I'd love to know. Maybe we could even throw quantitative tools at it. Is there any documented line from positivism to the (really rather terrible) fact/opinion worksheets American children still get in elementary school? They _look_ positivist to me, but it's possible that the origin comes from pragmatism, and especially Dewey. (Though thy do violate the opposition to dichotomies that Verhaegh says characterises later versions of pragmatism.) The conservative complaints in chapter 11 that positivists were separating facts and values would look really weird to students educated in the US over the last couple of generations.

I found especially pleasing in the book was the role that _public_ universities played in the story. The focus is so often on the famous Ivy League schools, and five of them are central to Verhaegh's book. But the story doesn't work without the public universities too. We see Schlick get a huge audience at Berkeley very early on, then Feigl gets hired by Iowa and given more resources at Minnesota. Reichenbach, after many challenges, is hired at UCLA. The central university at the end of the narrative, and still the most important positivist repository, is Pitt. And after Charles Stevenson is denied tenure at Yale, he gets a permanent home at Michigan, where I'm based. To this day, our most prestigious research prize for graduate students is the Stevenson prize.

I'll focus on a point where I only agree 90% with Verhaegh's narrative; philosophers can't help disagreeing. The short version is that I came away from the book thinking that the rise of analytic philosophy was a bit more inevitable, at least from around 1950, than he suggests. I think this is _at most_ a difference in emphasis, and it's the detailed evidence that he marshals about how it came about that convinced me.

So Chapter 9 is on, among other things, the spectacular rise of analytic philosophy in America post-WWII. As with all plausible narratives of this rise, Verhaegh's starts with the vexed question of just what this thing, analytic philosophy, is that ended up winning. The story he gives, and which he marshalls excellent evidence for, is that it becomes in effect the merger of the realist and positivist traditions. It's a merger of especially the Cambridge realist tradition with less doctrinaire versions of positivism. 

One really striking thing about the narrative is that the label, 'analytic philosophy', gets used for this would-be coalition before there is any sign of it being a coalition. It's a bit of what we'd now call conceptual engineering. And it's massively successful. The forces of 'scientific' philosophy really just run over all before them in the top American universities.

But it is such a weird coalition. This is why the definitional question is so hard. What exactly do Carnap, Moore, and Anscombe, have in common, which they don't also share with Peirce? Here Verhaegh also has a good pair of answers. First, what they have in common is a connection to _Russell_. One thing Verhaegh shows is that the positivists very consciously built a narrative where they were part of a common tradition with Russell, to fend off the charge that they were just a passing fad. Second, there seems to have been something almost deliberate about writing Peirce into the anti-canon.

Let's step back. One simple narrative, already visible at the time, was that pre-WWII there were four main factions in American philosophy: idealism, realism, pragmatism, and positivism. Maybe that's misleading, e.g., where do you put the Thomists, but it's helpful enough. If you're going to make a binary division from these four, realism plus positivism on one side is rather odd. 

You can see how positivism and pragmatism would go together. They are both anti-metaphysical. This led people to treat them similarly at the time. Verhaegh quotes Feigl, Morris, Nagel, and Hook as treating them as a pair. If they're different, where do you put Ramsey? Later in life, Ayer does this delightful interview with Bryan McGee where he says pragmatism was "very akin to" positivism. But this union doesn't work. Verhaegh suggests that it is because the pragmatists were allergic to dichotomies, like the fact/value one, and that seems like a good suggestion. Anyway, this pairing fails.

You can sort of see how positivism and idealism would go together. Especially in early versions of positivism, they both put conscious experience right at the center. Verhaegh quotes Carnap complaining that people were reading the _Aufbau_ as idealist. And maybe that's a misreading, but it suggests there could be some commonalities to build on. But that totally did not happen. (If it had happened, you can imagine Ayer vs Austin being the big dividing line in Anglophone philosophy.)

Instead, we get a positivist/realist coalition. Doctrinally, this seems very unstable. But it gets you Russell inside the coalition, without worrying about Russell's changes of views over the 1920s and 1930s. And it gets you logic and philosophy of science as central subjects. And that turned out to be enough.

Here's my contentious claim. Once that was the dividing line, the victory for the analytics was close to inevitable. We're taught to hate inevitability claims in history, and rightly so. And I do think it was really contingent that this became the dividing line. If Ramsey lives, maybe it doesn't happen. But once those are the sides, I think the analytics have to win. That's for two reasons. 

One is that idealism, especially in America, was dying. And pragmatism was just not strong enough to fight on its own. Verhaegh has some damning numbers on this. At the key moment, eleven of Columbia's thirteen faculty were homegrown. If Deweyan pragmatism had really been strong, there would have been graduate students so good you couldn't help hiring them. There weren't.

The other, and this comes back to the over-simplification of the four way division, is that forming this coalition left the opposing forces hopelessly divided. At Columbia, the anti-analytics wanted Deweyian pragmatism. At Princeton, they wanted Christian humanism. At Yale, they wanted "space for metaphysics". That's not a group. When analytic philosophy did face a threat, it was from 'continental philosophy'. Now continental philosophy, like analytic philosophy, covers a multitude of sins. But the advantage each has is that they'll work with a pretty broad range of others under the umbrella, at least for institution building. That's needed to fight a battle like this, and the 1950s anti-analytics didn't have it.

So I'll end with a question, one that I guess relates to the chapter 13 discussion of explanation. I think counterfactuals are crucial to explanation. If we want to explain why analytic philosophy became dominant, we need to ask what the philosophical world would looked like if it never became dominant. My question is, what does that world look like? And how late can it reasonably, feasibly, differ from actual history? My guess is that the deviation from actual history has to come relatively early; by 1950, the outcome is baked in, even though the analytics don't actually take over for several more years. But I'd like to be convinced I'm wrong; I get nervous with inevitability claims!

To wrap up, this is a fantastic book, full of insights on both the history of philosophy, and the methodology of that history. I hope it's really widely read.
